summary: Meridian is a free, browser-based explorer for NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey, designed for people who can move only their eyes, such as people with ALS or high spinal cord injury. The challenge data pose a precision problem: even the fastest-moving star, Barnard’s Star, shifts less than one 6.15″ SPHEREx pixel between six-month surveys, while webcam eye tracking errs by hundreds of screen pixels. Meridian solves this by dividing the work. Software performs the precise image comparison (time-lapse, blinking, differencing, 16-year WISE + SPHEREx motion trails, Gaia overlays and a spectral energy distribution built from Gaia DR3 spectra), and the user makes only a few large selections by gaze, keyboard, or an AI guide. We collected our own dataset of 50,000 labeled webcam frames from 10 people and trained a gaze model that reaches 225 px error on new people, lowered to 126–145 px with a short personal calibration. Using Meridian, we measured the motion of the coldest known brown dwarf, WISE 0855, at 8.2″/yr, matching its catalogue value of about 8.1″/yr. We tested every tool on the 5 challenge targets, and adding data is easy: any object can be searched by name, its SPHEREx images are fetched on demand from NASA’s archive and cached, and one command prepares new targets in advance. Every action works without a mouse, and the tool needs only an ordinary laptop.

What does it do?
Meridian is a free web app for exploring NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey. It is built so that a person who can move only their eyes, such as someone with ALS or a high spinal cord injury, can use every feature with an ordinary laptop webcam. Users fly across a 3D SPHEREx sky, switch between its 102 infrared bands (0.75–5.0 µm), zoom into any field, and open the real SPHEREx images to find objects that move or change. These include brown dwarfs, nearby stars, and the kind of cold, faint object a Planet X search looks for.

How does it work?
The principle is that software does the precise work and the user makes the decisions. This matters because Barnard’s Star, the fastest-moving known star, shifts only 0.83 SPHEREx pixel between surveys: Δx = μΔt / p (shift in pixels = proper motion × time between surveys ÷ pixel scale). Webcam gaze estimates, by contrast, miss by about 225 screen pixels.

  1. Gaze model. We recorded our own dataset: 10 volunteers, 5 sessions each, 50,000 labelled webcam frames, split by person. A small regression head on a frozen UniGaze vision transformer predicts where the user is looking. It reached 225 px mean error on two people it had never seen, against 300 px for the best baseline. A 100-point personal calibration that accounts for head pose and lighting cut live error to 126–145 px.
  2. Gaze control. The gaze moves a cursor across the whole screen, like a mouse. It is steadied by median and One Euro filters and snaps to nearby buttons. A 0.8 s look presses a control, with a visible progress bar; the time is adjustable from 0.4 to 1.5 s. Every control is at least 64 px, and nothing clickable sits near the screen edges.
  3. Detection views. Users can play a time-lapse, blink between dates, subtract images, or stack WISE/NEOWISE (2010–2024) and SPHEREx (2025–2026) images into a 16-year motion trail. They can also compare a field with Gaia DR3 star positions; a moving source with no Gaia match stands out as a candidate cold object.
  4. AI guide. A guide built on Claude (Anthropic) explains what the user is seeing in plain language. It can run tours that operate the interface, and it offers help after the user rests their gaze on a sky object for 7 seconds.

Every action is a named command, so gaze, keyboard and the AI guide have identical access.

Results

  • WISE 0855 (the coldest known brown dwarf): proper motion measured at 8.2″/yr, against the published 8.1″/yr, which is within about 1%. It was detected 14.8 standard deviations above the image noise in 258 SPHEREx frames.
  • Barnard’s Star: its motion was detected from one year of SPHEREx data alone.
  • All five challenge targets open offline in all eight viewing modes in under one second.

What benefits does it have?

  • Free. It runs in a web browser with a built-in webcam: no purchase, no special hardware. Clinical eye-gaze devices cost about US$8,395, and Medicare funds them only for severe speech impairment.
  • No mouse needed. Every feature works by gaze, keyboard or the AI guide.
  • No prior astronomy knowledge needed. The guide explains each object and view.

What is the intended impact?
ALS takes movement first, and with it independence and purpose. That loss feeds depression, and people with ALS face a several-fold higher suicide risk. Meridian gives back the ability to explore, learn and take part in real science. Discovery has never required hands: Pluto was found by comparing two images. The same tool serves people with ALS, spinal cord injury, locked-in syndrome or Parkinson’s: one solution, many targets. Its approach, precise software paired with coarse human input, can extend to other NASA archives and open citizen science to people who are currently excluded.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Front end: JavaScript (Vite) with Aladin Lite 3.8.2 (CDS Strasbourg).
  • Back end: Python (FastAPI, astropy, astroquery, reproject, NumPy) with an offline cache.
  • Gaze tracking: PyTorch with UniGaze-B/16, OpenCV YuNet and MediaPipe Face Landmarker.
  • AI guide: Claude (Anthropic).
  • Testing: Playwright for automated browser tests.
  • Hardware: a laptop with a 1,280 × 720 built-in webcam; an NVIDIA RTX 5060 laptop GPU for training.
  • Data: SPHEREx DR1 (NASA/JPL-Caltech, via NASA/IPAC IRSA); WISE/NEOWISE; CatWISE2020; Gaia DR3 (ESA).

How is it creative?
Webcam gaze is far less precise than a mouse, and SPHEREx motion is smaller than a pixel. Instead of fighting both problems, Meridian gives each to the side that can solve it: the computer makes the sub-pixel comparison across three missions, and the person brings the curiosity and the decisions. As far as we know, it is the first tool to put space-telescope survey data under eye-only control using an ordinary webcam.

What factors did we consider?

  • Scientific honesty. Modelled frames are labelled, simulations are called simulations, and published values are shown next to ours.
  • Consent and privacy. All volunteers gave written consent, and the data are stored locally under participant codes.
  • Fatigue. 23.3% of eye-tracker users with ALS limit use because of fatigue, so Meridian keeps selections few, lets users adjust the dwell time, and includes a rest zone to pause.
  • Limitations and next steps. Meridian has not yet been tested by people with ALS or tetraplegia. The dataset covers 10 people and one setup, and eye movement can decline in late-stage ALS. Next, we will test with these communities and extend the approach to other NASA surveys.
